subjective.question: Define Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). What is its main goal? (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Human-Computer Interaction is the discipline concerned with the design, evaluation and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use, and with the study of the major phenomena surrounding them. Its main goal is to develop interactive systems that are usable — effective, efficient, safe and satisfying for the people who use them.

subjective.question: Briefly explain the three input-output channels through which a human interacts with a computer. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: (1) Vision: the dominant channel; the eye receives light and perceives size, shape, colour, brightness, pattern and movement. (2) Hearing: the ear receives sound — pitch, loudness and timbre — and can process information in parallel with vision, e.g. warning sounds. (3) Touch (haptic): receptors in the skin and joints sense pressure, texture, position and movement of the fingers and limbs, giving feedback about key presses and pointing actions. The human's output is produced by motor actions such as pressing keys and moving a mouse.

subjective.question: Describe the three types of human memory. Give the capacity and duration of each. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: (1) Sensory memory: buffers attached to each sense (iconic for vision, echoic for hearing, haptic for touch). It has a very large capacity but information lasts only a fraction of a second to about 2 seconds before it decays or is passed on. (2) Short-term (working) memory: a scratch-pad for temporary recall. It holds about 7 ± 2 chunks of information (Miller's law), is accessed rapidly (about 70 ms) and information decays in roughly 15-30 seconds unless rehearsed. (3) Long-term memory: the repository of all our knowledge. Its capacity is vast, access is slower (about one-tenth of a second), and forgetting happens slowly; it stores episodic memory (events) and semantic memory (facts and concepts).

subjective.question: Differentiate between slips and mistakes in human error. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Slips are unintentional errors that occur during the execution of a correct intention — the plan is right but the action goes wrong, e.g. pressing the wrong key or clicking the wrong button. Mistakes occur through conscious deliberation: the intention or plan itself is wrong, e.g. a user deliberately deletes a file believing it is the correct one, or applies the wrong rule to a situation. In short, slips are failures of execution; mistakes are failures of intention/formation of the goal.

subjective.question: What is a mental model? Why is it important in interface design? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: A mental model is the internal representation or understanding that a user has of how a system works, built up from experience, training and the image the system presents. It is important because users act according to their mental model, not according to how the system actually works. If the designer's conceptual model is not communicated clearly through the system image, the user's mental model will be wrong and the user will make errors and find the system hard to learn and use.

subjective.question: Define attention. Differentiate between focused attention and divided attention. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Attention is the process of selecting things to concentrate on, at a point in time, from the range of possibilities available. Focused attention is the ability to concentrate on a single stimulus or task while ignoring others, e.g. reading a document in a noisy room. Divided attention is the ability to split attention between two or more tasks or stimuli at the same time, e.g. driving a car while listening to the radio. Divided attention is possible only when the tasks are well practised or use different channels.

subjective.question: Explain the three types of reasoning: deductive, inductive and abductive, with examples. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: (1) Deductive reasoning derives a logically necessary conclusion from given premises: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. Example: 'If it is raining then the ground is wet; it is raining, therefore the ground is wet.' (2) Inductive reasoning generalises from particular cases we have seen to all cases. Example: having seen many white swans, we conclude all swans are white. It is useful but unreliable, because the next case may break the pattern. (3) Abductive reasoning goes from an observed event back to the action or state that caused it, i.e. it explains events. Example: the computer screen is blank, so the user concludes the machine has crashed. Abduction is also unreliable, because the explanation chosen may be wrong (the screen may only be asleep).

subjective.question: What is the Problem Space Framework? State its main strength as a model of human problem solving. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: The Problem Space Framework (Newell and Simon) views problem solving as a search through a space of knowledge states: the solver starts in an initial state, applies operators (actions) to move from state to state, and tries to reach the goal state, using sub-goals where necessary. Its main strength is that it operates within the constraints of the human processing system — it models problem solving in a way that respects the limits of human memory and processing, which makes it a realistic model of how people actually solve problems.

subjective.question: Define usability. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Usability is the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use (ISO 9241). In simple words, a system is usable if it is easy to learn, efficient to use, easy to remember, causes few errors and is subjectively satisfying.

subjective.question: Explain the usability goals of an interactive system. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: (1) Effectiveness: a very general goal — how good a system is at doing what it is supposed to do. (2) Efficiency: the way a system supports users in carrying out their tasks, i.e. the resources (time, effort) expended in achieving the goals. (3) Safety: protecting the users from dangerous conditions and from undesired situations, e.g. preventing serious errors. (4) Utility: the extent to which the system provides the right kind of functionality so that users can do what they need to or want to do. (5) Learnability: how easy a system is to learn to use. (6) Memorability: how easy a system is to remember how to use, once it has been learned.

subjective.question: Differentiate between usability goals and user experience goals. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Usability goals are objective: they are concerned with whether the system meets specific usability criteria such as effectiveness and efficiency, and they can be assessed through measurable performance. User experience goals are subjective: they describe how the experience of using the system feels to the user — e.g. satisfying, enjoyable, engaging, pleasurable, exciting, motivating, aesthetically pleasing and emotionally fulfilling. User experience goals are therefore less clearly defined and cannot be measured as directly as usability goals.

subjective.question: What is the Usability Engineering Lifecycle? Who proposed it? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: The Usability Engineering Lifecycle was proposed by Deborah Mayhew. It is a structured approach to developing usable systems in three broad stages: (1) Requirements analysis — building user profiles, doing task analysis and setting measurable usability goals; (2) Design, testing and development — designing at increasing levels of detail and carrying out usability testing at each level, iterating the design; (3) Installation — collecting feedback from actual use. Its key features are setting quantitative usability goals early and testing iteratively against them.

subjective.question: Differentiate between formative evaluation and summative evaluation. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Formative evaluation is carried out during the design and development of a system, while it can still be changed. Its purpose is to find usability problems and improve the design, so it is done repeatedly with prototypes. Summative evaluation is carried out on a finished (or nearly finished) product. Its purpose is to assess whether the product meets the specified usability goals or benchmarks, and to compare it with competing products or standards.

subjective.question: What is heuristic evaluation? Who proposed it? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Heuristic evaluation is a usability inspection method proposed by Jakob Nielsen (with Rolf Molich). A small set of evaluators (typically 3-5) independently examine the interface and judge whether it complies with recognised usability principles called heuristics — such as visibility of system status, match between the system and the real world, user control and freedom, consistency and standards, and error prevention. The evaluators' findings are then combined. It is quick and cheap, needs no users, and finds a large proportion of usability problems.

subjective.question: What is usability testing? Explain how a usability test is conducted. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Usability testing is the evaluation of a system by having representative users perform representative tasks with it, while their performance and reactions are observed and recorded. A typical test is conducted as follows: (1) Define the goals of the test and the tasks/scenarios to be performed. (2) Select participants who represent the intended users. (3) Prepare the test material — task instructions, questionnaires and recording setup. (4) Conduct the sessions: the user performs the tasks, often thinking aloud, while observers record completion time, errors and difficulties; no help is given. (5) Measure satisfaction afterwards with questionnaires or interviews. (6) Analyse the results — where users failed or were slow, and why — and report the problems with recommendations for redesign.

subjective.question: What is interaction design? (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Interaction design is designing interactive products to support the way people communicate and interact in their everyday and working lives. In other words, it is about creating user experiences that enhance and augment the way people work, communicate and interact.

subjective.question: Explain Norman's execution-evaluation cycle (the seven stages of action). (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Norman's model describes an interaction as a cycle of seven stages. Execution side: (1) Establishing the goal — the user decides what to achieve. (2) Forming the intention — deciding to act to achieve the goal. (3) Specifying the action sequence — working out the exact operations needed. (4) Executing the action — actually performing the operations. Evaluation side: (5) Perceiving the state of the world — sensing what has happened. (6) Interpreting the state of the world — making sense of the feedback. (7) Evaluating the state of the world — comparing the outcome with the original goal and intention. The cycle then repeats with a new or refined goal until the task is complete.

subjective.question: Explain the gulf of execution and the gulf of evaluation. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: The gulf of execution is the difference between the intentions/goals of the user and the actions that the system allows the user to perform — it measures how easy it is to act on the system. The gulf of evaluation is the difference between the state of the system as presented to the user and the user's expectations — it measures how easy it is to perceive and interpret whether the goal has been achieved. A well-designed interface narrows (bridges) both gulfs, e.g. by providing direct, meaningful controls and clear feedback.

subjective.question: What does GOMS stand for? Explain its four components. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: GOMS stands for Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules; it is a model of human task performance given by Card, Moran and Newell. (1) Goals: what the user wants to achieve. (2) Operators: the basic perceptual, motor and cognitive actions the user performs, e.g. pressing a key or moving the mouse. (3) Methods: procedures made of sequences of operators and sub-goals that accomplish a goal. (4) Selection rules: the rules by which the user chooses among the competing methods available for a goal. GOMS is used to predict how long an expert user will take to perform a task.

subjective.question: What are personas in goal-directed design? Explain the types of personas. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: A persona is a fictional, archetypal representation of a class of real users, created from research into users' behaviour patterns, goals, skills, attitudes and environment, and given a name, face and personal details so that designers can design for a specific 'person' instead of a vague 'user'. Types of personas: (1) Primary persona: the main target of the design; the interface is designed primarily for this persona, and it cannot be satisfied by an interface designed for another persona. (2) Secondary persona: also uses the product; most of its needs are met by the primary interface but it has additional specific needs that must be addressed without disturbing the primary design. (3) Served persona: not an actual user of the product, but directly/indirectly affected by its use, e.g. a manager who receives reports produced by others using the system. (4) Supplemental persona: its needs are a combination of primary and secondary needs and it is fully satisfied by the primary interface. (5) Negative (exclusionary) persona: a user type for whom the product is explicitly NOT being designed.

subjective.question: What are scenarios in goal-directed design? Name their types. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: A scenario is a narrative story describing a specific instance of use: a persona, in a specific context, with specific goals, carrying out specific tasks with the product. Scenarios let designers explore and communicate how the product will be used before it is built. In goal-directed design three types are used: (1) Context scenarios — broad, day-in-the-life stories used to explore the product concept and derive requirements. (2) Key path scenarios — detailed descriptions of the persona's primary, most frequent interactions, used to refine the design. (3) Validation scenarios — 'what-if' stories covering less frequent and edge-case situations, used to test the design.

subjective.question: What is meant by affordance? Give an example. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Affordance refers to the perceived and actual properties of an object that suggest how it can be used. For example, a button on a screen looks raised and clickable, so it affords pushing/clicking; a door handle affords pulling, while a flat plate affords pushing. Good affordances make the correct action obvious without instructions.

subjective.question: Explain the phases of the goal-directed design process. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: (1) Research: understand the domain and the users through interviews, observation and literature review. (2) Modelling: synthesise the research into models — above all personas, and workflow models of how work is done. (3) Requirements definition: using context scenarios, identify each persona's goals and needs and define the product requirements. (4) Interaction framework: define the overall structure of the product — its form factor, screens/views, functional groups and the basic behaviour of the interface. (5) Refinement: work out the design in full detail — detailed behaviour, look and feel, and information design. (6) Development support: support the developers during implementation, adjusting the design where technical constraints require it, without losing the design vision.

subjective.question: Explain the waterfall model of the software lifecycle. Why is it not suitable for interactive systems? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: The waterfall model is a linear, sequential lifecycle model in which each phase — requirements, design, implementation, testing and maintenance — must be completed before the next phase can start. It is not suitable for interactive systems because the users' needs and the usability of the interface can only be discovered by trying designs with users; in the waterfall model feedback comes only after implementation, when changes are very expensive. Interactive system design therefore needs an iterative cycle of prototyping and evaluation, which the waterfall model does not allow.

subjective.question: Differentiate between standards and guidelines in HCI. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Standards are authoritative requirements produced by national or international bodies (e.g. ISO 9241). They are usually specific, measurable and sometimes legally enforceable, and they tend to deal with matters such as health, safety and performance. Guidelines are recommendations and best-practice advice drawn from research and expert experience (e.g. Shneiderman's golden rules or the Smith and Mosier guidelines). They are more general and flexible than standards, cover a wider range of design issues, and must be interpreted and applied by the designer rather than obeyed literally.

subjective.question: Explain the star lifecycle model of Hartson and Hix. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The star lifecycle is a model of interactive system development proposed by Hartson and Hix. The activities of development — task/functional analysis, requirements specification, conceptual and formal design, prototyping, and implementation — are arranged as the points of a star, and evaluation is placed at the centre of the star. The designer may begin at any point and move from any activity to any other, but every move passes through evaluation at the centre: whatever is produced is evaluated before work proceeds. The model therefore emphasises that interactive development is evaluation-driven and iterative rather than a fixed sequence of phases.

subjective.question: List and briefly explain Shneiderman's eight golden rules of interface design. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: (1) Strive for consistency: similar situations should use similar sequences of actions, terminology and layout. (2) Enable frequent users to use shortcuts: abbreviations, function keys and macros speed up expert work (cater to universal usability). (3) Offer informative feedback: every user action should produce visible system feedback. (4) Design dialogs to yield closure: sequences of actions should have a beginning, middle and end, with feedback confirming completion. (5) Offer error prevention and simple error handling: design so errors cannot occur, and where they do, give simple instructions to correct them. (6) Permit easy reversal of actions: undo facilities relieve anxiety and encourage exploration. (7) Support internal locus of control: make the user feel in charge of the system, not responding to it. (8) Reduce short-term memory load: keep displays simple and avoid making the user remember information from one screen to the next.

subjective.question: What is prototyping? Differentiate between low-fidelity and high-fidelity prototypes. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Prototyping is building a preliminary, partial version of a system so that design ideas can be explored and evaluated with users early, before the real system is built. A low-fidelity prototype is rough and cheap — e.g. paper sketches or storyboards; it is quick to produce and change, and is used to test concepts and layout. A high-fidelity prototype looks and behaves much like the final product, usually built in software; it is used to test detailed design, but it costs more time and effort and users may mistake it for the finished system.

subjective.question: Explain the main interaction styles used in interactive systems. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: (1) Command language: the user types commands (e.g. DOS commands). It is powerful and flexible for experts but hard to learn and remember. (2) Menus: the user selects from a list of options displayed by the system; it replaces recall with recognition, so it is easy for novices, but can be slow for experts. (3) Form fill-in: the user fills fields on a screen form, as on a paper form; suitable for data entry. (4) Direct manipulation: the user manipulates on-screen objects directly with a pointing device (dragging, resizing icons and windows); actions are visible, incremental and reversible. (5) Natural language: the user speaks or types in ordinary language; it needs no special learning but suffers from ambiguity. (Question-and-answer dialogs, in which the system asks questions and the user answers, are another simple style used in wizards.)

subjective.question: What is direct manipulation? State its features/advantages. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Direct manipulation is an interaction style, identified by Shneiderman, in which the user acts directly on visible objects on the screen instead of typing commands. Its features are: (1) continuous representation of the objects of interest; (2) physical actions and labelled buttons instead of complex syntax; (3) rapid, incremental, reversible operations whose effect on the object is immediately visible. Its advantages are that it is easy to learn and remember, produces fewer errors, encourages exploration, and gives users a high level of satisfaction and sense of control.

subjective.question: What is a WIMP interface? Name its four components. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: WIMP stands for Windows, Icons, Menus and Pointers. It is the standard graphical user interface paradigm: Windows are separate areas of the screen used for different tasks or documents; Icons are small pictures representing objects and actions; Menus offer choices of operations and services on the screen; and the Pointer is the cursor, moved by a pointing device such as a mouse, used to select and manipulate objects.

subjective.question: Explain any three types of menus used in graphical interfaces. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: (1) Pull-down menus: when the user selects a title in the menu bar at the top of the screen, the menu drops down and the user selects an item from it. (2) Pop-up menus: menus that appear at the pointer's position when invoked (e.g. by a right-click); they are context-sensitive and remain hidden until needed. (3) Cascading menus: a menu item with an arrow opens a further sub-menu to its side, giving a hierarchy of choices. (Pie menus, in which items are arranged in a circle around the pointer, are another type.)

subjective.question: State Fitts' law and explain its implication for interface design. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Fitts' law predicts the time taken to move to and select a target: MT = a + b log2(D/W + 1), where D is the distance from the starting point to the target and W is the width (size) of the target. The design implication is that the time to acquire a target decreases if the target is larger and/or closer. Therefore frequently used controls should be made large and placed close to where the pointer usually is; controls at the edges and corners of the screen are fastest to reach because they behave as if infinitely large; and small, distant targets should be avoided.

subjective.question: What are icons? State the characteristics of good icons. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Icons are small pictures or images displayed on the screen that represent objects, functions or actions, which the user can select to invoke the associated operation. Good icons are: familiar and easy to recognise; clear and unambiguous in meaning; consistent in style with the other icons in the system; clearly distinguishable from one another; of suitable size; and, where the meaning is not obvious, supported by a text label or tooltip.

subjective.question: Explain the different types of keyboards: QWERTY, Dvorak, alphabetical and chord keyboards. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: (1) QWERTY keyboard: the standard layout, inherited from typewriters; almost all users are trained on it, so it remains dominant despite not being optimal. (2) Dvorak keyboard: a layout designed for speed and efficiency, placing the most frequently used letters under the strongest fingers; it can give faster typing, but the cost of retraining keeps it rare. (3) Alphabetical keyboard: keys arranged in alphabetical order; it looks easier for beginners, but in practice gives no advantage and is slower for experienced users. (4) Chord keyboard: only a few keys, and a character is entered by pressing several keys at once (in combination, like a piano chord). Chord keyboards are very small and fast after training, but difficult to learn; they are used in specialised devices.

subjective.question: Define Recognition
subjective.answer: Recognition refers to act of recognizing or the state of being recognized, identification of something as having been previously seen, heard, and known as.

subjective.question: what is the difference between Tertiary and Analogous colors?
subjective.answer: These are the colors formed by mixing one primary and one secondary color. TERTIARY COLORS Yellow-orange, red-orange, red-purple, blue-purple, blue-green and yellow-green. Analogous colors are any three colors, which are side by side on a 12 part color wheel, Such as yellow-green, yellow, and yellow-orange. Usually one of the three colors Predominates

subjective.question: Comment to justify the following statement. "Most users are neither beginners nor experts; instead they are intermediates" What are the pointing devices? Explain trackball as pointing device?
subjective.answer: According to the statement pointing devices will help for the beginner user because we can use to deal easily with requirement. Pointing devices are input devices that can be used to specify a point or path in a one-, Two- or three- dimensional space and, like keyboards, their characteristics have to be considering in relation to design needs. Pointing devices are as follow: • Mouse • Touch pad • Track ball • Joystick • Touch screen • Eye gaze Trackballs is other alternatives. The user is presented with a cursor on the screen that is controlled by the input device.

subjective.question: Consider the vertical scroll bar of a web browser or word processor. For each of Norman's five principles below, give one way that the scrollbar uses the principle for effective design. Describe the interface model of the scroll bar in one sentence. [2*5] Affordance: Constraints: Mapping: Visibility: Feedback:
subjective.answer: Affordance is a term used to refer to an attribute of an object that allows people to know How to use it. For example, a mouse button invites pushing by the way it is physically constrained in its plastic shell. At a very simple level, to afford means "to give a clue." When the affordances of a physical object are perceptually obvious it is easy to know how to interact with it Constraints: The design concept of constraining refers to determining ways of restricting the kind of user interaction that can take place at a given moment. There are various ways this can be achieved. An Interface design in graphical user interfaces is to deactivate certain menu options by shading them, thereby restricting the user to only actions permissible at that stage of the activity. Physical constraints Physical constraints refer to the way physical objects restrict the movement of things. Logical constraints Logical constraints rely on people's understanding of the way the world works Culture constraints Culture constraints rely on learned conventions, like the use of red for warning, the use of certain kinds of signals for danger, and the use of the smiley face to represent happy emotions Mapping: This refers to the relationship between controls and their effects in the world. Nearly all artifacts need some kind of mapping between controls and effects, whether it is a flashlight, car, power plant, or cockpit. An example of a good mapping between controls is effect is the up and down arrows used to represent the up and down movement of the cursor, respectively, on a computer keyboard. Visibility: The more visible functions are, the more likely users will be able to know what to do next. In contrast, when functions are "out of sight," it makes them more difficult to fid and knows how to use. Norman describes the controls of a car to emphasize this point. The controls for different operations are clearly visible (e.g., indicator, headlights, horn, hazard warning lights), indicating what can be done. Feedback Related to the concept of visibility is feedback. This is best illustrated by an analogy to what everyday life would be like without it. Imagine trying to play a guitar, slice bread using knife, or write a pen if none of the actions produced any effect for several seconds. There would be an unbearable delay before the music was produced, the bread was cut, or the words appeared on the paper, making it almost impossible for the person to continue with the next strum, saw, or stroke. Feedback is about sending back information about what action has been done and what has been accomplished, allowing the person to continue with the activity. Various kinds of feedback are available for interaction design—audio, tactile, verbal, visual, and combinations of these.

subjective.question: As a product designer what you need to do for constructing personas. Write all steps
subjective.answer: Being a product designer we use to do constructing personas steps:- 1. Revisit the persona hypothesis 2. Map interview subjects to behavioral variables 3. Identify significant behavior patterns 4. Synthesize characteristics and relevant goals. 5. Check for completeness. 6. Develop narratives 7. Designate persona types

subjective.question: Suppose you are a product designer and have to create a product that satisfies a broad audience. What user-centered design issues arise during product development, and how do personas resolve them?
subjective.answer: Being a product designer keeping in the mind before we going to create a product that satisfy board audience in self referential design which are given : Personas To create a product that must satisfy a broad audience of users, logic tells you to make it as broad in its functionality as possible to accommodate the most people. This logic, however, is flawed. The best way to successfully accommodate a variety of users is to design for specific types of individuals with specific needs. Personas also resolve three User-Centered design issues that arise during product development: The elastic user Self-referential design Design edge cases The elastic user Although satisfying the user is goal, the term user causes trouble when applied to specific design problems and contexts. Its imprecision makes it unusable as a design tool—every person on a product team has his own conceptions of the user and what the user needs. Self-referential design Self-referential design occurs when designers or developers project their own goals, motivations, skills, and mental models onto a product's design. Most "cool" product designs fall into this category: the audience doesn't extend beyond people like the designer, which is fine for a narrow range of products and completely inappropriate for most others. Similarly, programmers apply self-referential design when they create implementation-model products. They understand perfectly how it works and are comfortable with such products. Few non- programmers would concur. Design edge cases Another syndrome that personas help prevent is designing for edge cases—those situations that might possibly happen, but usually won't for the target personas. Naturally, edge cases must be programmed for, but they should never be the design focus. Personas provide a reality check for the design.

subjective.question: Being a researcher, identify in which phases of ethnographic interviews you Explore, Identify patterns of use and Confirm patterns of use? Briefly explain them. 3 marks
subjective.answer: Being researcher ethnography is term borrowed form anthropology, meaning the systematic and immersive study of human cultures. In anthropology, ethnographic researchers spend years living immersed in the cultures they study and record. Ethnographic interviews take the spirit of this type of research and apply it on a micro level. Rather than trying to understand behaviors and social ritual of an entire culture, the goal is understand the behaviors and rituals of people interacting with individual products. Identifying candidates The personal hypothesis

subjective.question: being a researcher, what is the need of literature review in research in your point of view? Give brief answer. 2 marks
subjective.answer: In parallel with stakeholder interviews, the design team should review any literature pertaining to the product or its domain. This can and should include product marketing plans, market research, technology specifications and white papers, business and technical journal articles in the domain, competitive studies. Web searches for related and competing products and news, usability study results and metrics, and customer support data such as call center statistics.

subjective.question: List four kinds of translated input events. 2 marks
subjective.answer: 1. Mouse click or double-click 2. Mouse entered or exited component 3. Keyboard focus gained or lost 4. Character typed

subjective.question: what is a semantic network
subjective.answer: Semantic memory is structured in some way to allow access to information, representation of relationships between pieces of information, and inference. One model for the way in which semantic memory is structured is as a network. Items are associated to each other in classes, and may inherit attributes from parent classes. This model is known as a semantic network

subjective.question: Why the user are blamed themselves for guilty the insomnious or faults? 5 marks
subjective.answer: User can blamed badly designed objects—constructed so as to lead to misunderstanding—faulty mental models, and poor feedback, no wonder people feel guilty when they have trouble using objects, especially when they perceive that nobody else is having the same problems. The problem is that once failure starts, it soon generalizes by self-blame to all technology. The vicious cycle starts: if you fail at something, you think it is your fault. Therefore you think you can't do that task. As a result, next time you have to do the task, you believe you can't so you don't even try. The result is that you can't, just as you thought. You are trapped in a self-fulfilling prophecy.

subjective.question: briefly explains physical constraints?
subjective.answer: Physical constraints refer to the way physical objects restrict the movement of things. For example, the way external disk can be placed into a disk drive is physically constrained by its shape and size, so that it can be inserted in only one way. Likewise, keys on a pad can usually be pressed in only one way.

subjective.question: usefulness of metaphor
subjective.answer: There are several dimensions along which the usefulness of a metaphor can be evaluated. A good metaphor, for example, might help the developers understand and agree on the functionality of the system they are designing.

subjective.question: How customer goal are different from corporate goal with respect to Non User Goal?
subjective.answer: Customer goals, corporate goals, and technical goals are all non-user goals. Typically, these goals must be acknowledged and considered, but they do not form the basis for the design direction. Although these goals need to be addressed, they must not be addressed at the expense of the use

subjective.question: Why dialog boxes are used in WIMP explain it with an example
subjective.answer: There are also many additional interaction objects and techniques commonly used in WIMP interfaces, some designed for specific purposes and others more general. Our discussion will cover the toolbars, menus, buttons, palettes and dialog boxes. Together, these elements of the WIMP interfaces are called widgets, and they comprise the toolkit for interaction between user and system. Example Normal pointer cursor maybe an arrow, but change to change to cross-hairs when drawing a line. Cursors are also used to tell the user about system activity.

subjective.question: Where do you use check boxes and radio buttons?
subjective.answer: Radio buttons: Buttons can also be used to toggle between two states, displaying status information such as whether the current font is italicized or not in a word processor or selecting options on a web form. Check boxes: It a set of options is not mutually exclusive, such as font characteristics like bold, italic and underlining, and then a set of toggle buttons can be used to indicate the on/off status of the options.

subjective.question: Describe the following design principles with examples and explain their implications for interface design: Visibility, Affordance.
subjective.answer: Visibility: The more visible functions are, the more likely users will be able to know what to do next. In contrast, when functions are —out of sight, it makes them more difficult to fid and knows how to use. Norman describes the controls of a car to emphasize this point. The controls for different operations are clearly visible (e.g., indicator, headlights, horn, hazard warning lights), indicating what can be done. Affordance is a term used to refer to an attribute of an object that allows people to know How to use it. For example, a mouse button invites pushing by the way it is physically constrained in its plastic shell. At a very simple level, to afford means —to give a clue. When the affordances of a physical object are perceptually obvious it is easy to know how to interact with it

subjective.question: Define Task?
subjective.answer: Tasks are the operation to manipulate the concepts of a domain. A goal is the desired output from a performed task. For example, one task within the graphic design domain is the construction of a specific geometric shape with particular attributes on the drawing surface.

subjective.question: Which model involve in risk analysis and prototyping?
subjective.answer: The spiral lifecycle model the spiral model of software development. Two features of the spiral model are immediately clear from figure: risk analysis and prototyping. The spiral model incorporates them in an iterative framework that allows ideas and progress to be repeatedly checked and evaluated. Each iteration around the spiral may be based on a different lifecycle model and may have different activities

subjective.question: Write the Problems of speech input.
subjective.answer: speech input suffers from a number of problems: • Speech input has been applied only in very specialized and highly constrained tasks. • Speech recognizers have severe limitations whereas a human would have a little problem distinguishing between similar sounding words or phrases; speech recognition systems are likely to make mistakes. • Speech recognizers are also subject to interference from background noise, although the use of a telephone-style handset or a headset may overcome this. • Even if the speech can be recognized, the natural form of language used by people is very difficult for a computer to interpret.
